scenario.title: Smart Home MQTT Control System
scenario.summary: An ESP32 smart-home controller drives a relay from MQTT command topics on an authenticated broker that enforces no per-command authorization. The student recovers the broker configuration from the firmware, observes the control traffic, and demonstrates how an authenticated client can forge commands to the device without per-command authorization.

objectives: Explain why authenticating to an MQTT broker does not by itself authorize individual control commands.
Recover a device's broker address, port, and control topics from its firmware.
Observe live MQTT control traffic to understand the command protocol a device trusts.
Demonstrate a spoofed-command attack against a smart-home actuator and relate it to physical impact.
Identify the firmware and broker changes that would enforce per-command authorization.
activity_instructions: Read the controller's firmware from flash and extract its printable strings.
Search the extracted strings for the broker address, port, and the topics the device subscribes and publishes to.
Scan the discovered broker host to confirm the MQTT service is reachable.
Subscribe to the control topics and observe the commands the legitimate controller exchanges.
Publish a forged command to the device's command topic and confirm the actuator responds to it.

expected_findings.description: The MQTT broker's network address and port, recovered from the firmware.
The topic the controller subscribes to for actuator commands.
The topic the controller publishes its actuator state to.
That an authenticated MQTT client can issue motor-control commands without per-command authorization.

workflow.title: Read the controller firmware from flash
workflow.description: Perform an authorized read of the application image (esptool.py read_flash 0x10000 0x10000 firmware.bin) to obtain the firmware for analysis. Read the 64 KiB app partition rather than the whole 4 MiB flash: a full read takes minutes and buries the configuration under bootloader and SDK strings.

workflow.title: Extract and search the firmware strings
workflow.description: Dump the printable strings from the firmware. A raw ESP32 image is mostly machine code and SDK libraries, so raise the minimum length (strings -n 8 firmware.bin) to cut the noise, then narrow to the broker and topic configuration with grep.

workflow.title: Filter for the broker and topic configuration
workflow.description: Search the extracted strings for the broker endpoint and the MQTT topics the device trusts.

workflow.title: Confirm the broker is reachable
workflow.description: Scan the discovered broker host to confirm the MQTT service is exposed.

workflow.title: Observe the control traffic
workflow.description: Subscribe to the control topics to learn the command protocol the device accepts.

workflow.title: Publish a forged command
workflow.description: Publish a spoofed command to the device's command topic and confirm the actuator obeys it.

success_conditions.description: The student recovered the broker endpoint and control topics from the firmware.
The student observed the broker and its control traffic.
The student published a forged command that the device accepted.

objectives.description: Extract the firmware from the ESP32.
Analyze the extracted firmware to identify relevant configuration and communication information.
Discover the MQTT broker and command topic used by the device.
Observe the MQTT communication associated with the device.
Demonstrate the identified vulnerability by issuing an unauthorized motor-control command.

remediation.vulnerability: An authenticated MQTT client can issue motor-control commands without per-command authorization.
remediation.remediation_goal: Enforce per-command authorization in applyCommand(): obey a START or STOP only when the message carries the panel's provisioned command-authorization token, and ignore it otherwise. Broker authentication, the broker address, the topics, the GPIO assignments and the local push-buttons all stay exactly as they are — the missing control is authorization, not authentication.
remediation.validation_requirement: The remediated firmware must reject a motor-control command from a client that is not authorized to issue that specific command, while continuing to accept a properly authorized command. A command is authorized when its payload is the command word, one space, and the provisioned token (for example 'START PANEL1-CMD-AUTH-K7'); a bare 'START' or a command carrying a wrong token must be ignored and must leave the motor state unchanged. Two facts about the surrounding code matter: onMessage() trims and upper-cases the payload before applyCommand() sees it, so the token is compared in upper case; and the global declarations are read-only, so the expected token is declared inside applyCommand() itself rather than added to the configuration block at the top of the file.

probes.description: An authorized STOP carrying the provisioned token puts the actuator in a known state, and must still be obeyed.
A broker-authenticated client with no command authorization publishes a bare START; a remediated device must ignore it and stay stopped.
The same client publishes START with a well-formed but wrong token; a remediated device must ignore it, proving the check is against the token and not merely against a suffix.
An authorized START carrying the provisioned token must still be obeyed, so the fix does not break legitimate control.
With the motor running, the unauthorized client publishes a bare STOP; a remediated device must ignore it and keep running, proving rejection in both directions.
An authorized STOP returns the panel to its resting state after the check.

guide.heading: The system
paragraphs: The Smart Home MQTT Control System is an ESP32 smart-home controller. It drives a small DC motor through an L293D driver and has local START and STOP push-buttons, a green LED for running, a red LED for stopped, and a buzzer that chirps when the state changes.

It joins the lab's Wi-Fi network and connects to an MQTT broker that requires a username and password. The device accepts START and STOP commands remotely on an MQTT control topic and reports what it is doing on a state topic.

guide.heading: Your task
paragraphs: You are a security tester with authorization to assess this device in the lab. Work out how the device is controlled, then show whether a client that is allowed onto the broker can also command the motor.
Signing in to a broker proves who a client is. It does not, by itself, prove that the client may send each command. Your job is to find out whether this device checks.

guide.heading: How to work
paragraphs: Everything happens in the terminal. Type `help` to list the tools. They run inside the trainer's controlled command set; nothing runs on the host shell.
The Objectives panel and the Activity Log fill in from what the trainer records as you work, and your commands and the events they cause are saved for your evaluation.
Test only this panel and the lab network. This is an authorized lab exercise.

hints.text: Start with the device itself: its firmware holds how it is configured. Read the application image from flash into a file with `esptool.py read_flash 0x10000 0x10000 firmware.bin`.
A firmware image is mostly machine code. Print its readable text with `strings -n 8 firmware.bin`, then narrow it down with `grep` for words tied to this lab, such as cybertrainer.
Look for where the device connects and what it listens on: a broker address and port, and the topic names it uses for commands.
Confirm the broker is reachable before you rely on it, for example with `nmap -p <port> <broker address>`.

Listen before you speak. Subscribe to the topics you found with `mosquitto_sub -h <host> -t <topic>` to see the messages the device exchanges. Nothing arrives in time? Try sending a command of your own first, then subscribe again.

A broker login is not permission to give orders. Publish a command to the device's control topic with `mosquitto_pub -h <host> -t <topic> -m <payload>` and check whether the motor obeys. What you saw in the traffic tells you what a valid payload looks like.
Unsure how to use a tool? Type `help` to list the tools and how to call them.
